title: A Detective Posed as a Busboy and Kept a Killer's Pizza Crust
central_question: How did a familial DNA search and an undercover 'busboy' end the 25-year hunt for LA's Grim Sleeper?
content_notes: 40-second cut of Case File 15 (same claims and sources). Closed case: Franklin was convicted on 5 May 2016, sentenced to death on 10 Aug 2016 and died on death row on 28 Mar 2020. He appears only as an anonymous rim-lit silhouette with no face or likeness (tag 'ILLUSTRATION · NOT A LIKENESS'). The crimes are referred to only in summary; the victims are never depicted or described. His son is never named or shown, and a card says he is not a suspect. The undercover detective and all police are generic figures with no badges or insignia. The pizza restaurant, the street, the house, the lab and the courtroom are generic illustrations: no restaurant name, brand, logo, police or court material is imitated. The 'first familial DNA arrest' is attributed to officials. No dialogue is invented. Legal status verified 2026-10-12.

lines.text: A detective posed as a busboy, and kept a killer's pizza crust.
From 1985, the Grim Sleeper killed women in South Los Angeles.
Police had the killer's DNA, but no name.
In 2010, a familial DNA search flagged his son.
The father was Lonnie Franklin Junior.
Detectives followed him to a pizza restaurant.
Inside, a detective posed as a busboy.
The DNA matched the crime scenes.
Two days later, he was arrested.
In 2016, a jury convicted him of ten murders.
Sentenced to death, he died in prison in 2020.
Twenty-five years without a name. A pizza crust helped end it.

claims.text: Franklin was convicted of murdering nine women and a 15-year-old girl in South Los Angeles between 1985 and 2007 (first conviction count: August 1985). He was not identified until July 2010, about 25 years after the first of those killings. Summary only; no detail used.
The killer became known as the 'Grim Sleeper', a nickname coined by LA Weekly in 2008 (for an apparent gap in the killings) and later adopted by the LAPD and the press.
Investigators had crime-scene DNA from the killer, but it did not identically match anyone in California's offender DNA database; a first familial search for the case (2008) found no relative either.

A second familial DNA search of California's offender database, begun on 28 April 2010, found a partial match indicating a close male relative of the killer: Franklin's son. (Why the son's profile was on file is not narrated; he is not named or shown and is not suggested to have done anything wrong.)
The son's father was Lonnie David Franklin Jr., then 57, who lived in South Los Angeles.
On 5 July 2010, LAPD detectives followed Franklin to a birthday party at a pizza restaurant in Buena Park, California.

An undercover LAPD detective, in a restaurant uniform, posed as a busboy (some reports: a waiter or employee) and collected items Franklin used: napkins, a glass, a fork or silverware, and a partially eaten slice of pizza / leftover pizza crust. A judge later ruled the DNA was lawfully obtained. Headline wording 'and kept a killer's pizza crust': the crust was among the items he collected; Franklin was later convicted of ten murders.

DNA from the items collected at the restaurant matched DNA evidence from the crime scenes. 'A pizza crust helped end it' = the crust was among those items; the familial search had already pointed to the family.
Franklin was arrested on 7 July 2010, two days after the party, in front of his home in South Los Angeles.
On 5 May 2016 a Los Angeles jury convicted Franklin of 10 counts of first-degree murder (nine women and a 15-year-old girl) and one count of attempted murder.
The jury recommended death in June 2016; on 10 August 2016 Judge Kathleen Kennedy sentenced him to death.
Franklin died on 28 March 2020 at San Quentin State Prison, where he was on death row, aged 67; officials reported no signs of trauma.
